title: Is Manu the Hindu rulebook?
hookLine: a guy online calls the Manusmriti the Hindu rulebook. is it?
carry: dharma has four sources, not one book
tomorrow: Priya has to pick one text to read critically for class. which?
last: THE AGE OF TRUTH COMES ROUND AGAIN.

lines: REAL, OLD, AND HARD TO READ.
WHAT DO YOU DO WITH IT?
cards: A guy in Priya's comments keeps quoting the same old book at her, verse numbers and all, as if that settles every argument: it's in the Hindu rulebook. The book is the Manusmriti, the laws of Manu.
It's real, it's old, and some of it is hard to read. But is it the Hindu rulebook? The book itself points somewhere else first.
So today's question: what do you do with an old book that says hard things?

teach.b: Start with what it is: a dharma text in verse, on duties, marriage, kings, food, purity and punishment.
The tradition calls it smriti, and Manu itself says the Veda is shruti and books like this one are smriti, set beside it. Now the hard part, said plainly.

teach.h: IT RANKS BY BIRTH. SOME PUSH BACK.
teach.b: It ranks people by the family they're born into and sets harsher rules for those lower down, and some of its verses limit women's freedom.
Some Hindus, reformers among them, have challenged it hard, and some reject it outright. Here's the tradition's own answer, from inside the book.
In its second chapter, Manu names where dharma comes from: the Veda first, then tradition, then the conduct of good people, and last, what sits right with one's own self.

teach.h: DHARMA HAS FOUR SOURCES, NOT ONE BOOK.
teach.b: That's the Hindu teaching to hold: dharma has four sources, not one book. So even this law book doesn't ask to be read alone. It gives a reader four places to stand, and one of them is conscience.
A neighbor tradition knows this problem well. The Torah says, "eye for eye, tooth for tooth."

teach.h: EYE FOR EYE, READ AS PAYMENT.
teach.b: The rabbis of the Talmud read it as payment for the injury, not a matching wound. That's the shared thing: a hard line in an old law, read by a later community with care, not just repeated.
And the honest difference: in Jewish tradition, the rabbis' reading became part of the law itself.
Hindu tradition has no single court for Manu; teachers and families keep, reshape or set aside its rules in different ways.

teach.h: READ IT WHOLE. SAY WHAT IT SAYS.
teach.b: Read it whole. Say what it says. Then weigh it.

how: Hindus relate to the Manusmriti in different ways: some cite parts of it, many teachers read it alongside other dharma texts and the Veda, and some Hindus, reformers among them, reject it.

o: the oldest collection of hymns in the Vedas
an old dharma text in verse, the laws of Manu
a book of Krishna's sayings to the warrior Arjuna

games.q: where Manu says dharma comes from — tap the pairs.
p: what sits right with one's own self

s: the hard verses people quote from Manu are made up
hard verses really are there; reading critically starts by saying so.
Manu lists what sits right with one's own self as a source of dharma
the Veda, tradition, the conduct of the good, and one's own self.
the rabbis of the Talmud read 'eye for eye' as payment for the injury
not a matching wound: a later community reading a hard line with care.

games.q: your uncle says: if it's in Manu, it's dharma, end of story. by Manu's own list, what's the fair reply?
o: Manu itself names four sources: the Veda, tradition, good people's conduct, and one's own self.
he's right: Manu names itself as the one and only source of dharma.
nothing old counts: dharma now is only whatever each person feels.
games.why: Manu 2.6 and 2.12 put the Veda first and end with what sits right with one's own self. Even the law book points past itself.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write two short lines: one rule you grew up with that you keep, and one you've questioned. Set them side by side and look at both for the sit, breathing slowly. Nothing needs deciding yet.

wordCard.voice: The Manusmriti: the laws of Manu, an old dharma text in verse; a smriti, set beside the Veda, with hard verses and its own list of where dharma comes from.

orig.note: Sanskrit Manusmriti: the smriti, the dharma tradition, of Manu.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma has four sources, not one book. Read Manu whole, say what it says, and let conscience have its say too. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Manusmriti 2.6 and 2.12 (the sources of dharma: the Veda, tradition, the conduct of the virtuous, and what satisfies one's own self)
Manusmriti 2.10 (shruti is the Veda; smriti the dharma texts)
Manusmriti 1.87–91 (duties assigned to the four varnas by birth)
